newsitem.title: USA: DC board to U.S. lawmakers - Put up or shut up.
newsitem.headline: DC board to U.S. lawmakers - Put up or shut up.

text.p: District of Columbia's financial control board is about to put the U.S. Congress on notice that the district will collapse unless Capitol Hill assumes annual payment of $1 billion in city services, a board member said Tuesday.
Stephen Harlan, vice chairman of the congressionally mandated board, said the panel will issue the warning in a blunt "strategic planning report" due out this week.

The report will warn Congress that its 1974 decision to hand over Medicaid, corrections, mental health and pension programs to the District under a new Home Rule agreement has failed, Harlan told a D.C. Institute of CPAs meeting.
"This thing won't work. It's fundamentally flawed and broken," said Harlan, a former chair of KPMG Peat Marwick. He said that "D.C. was grossly mistreated" under the 1974 plan.

Harlan said this week's report has a chilling message for Capitol Hill. "If you don't help us, we are going to give the keys back, because it's your problem," said Harlan, noting that some District programs are in a "shambles."
"The federal government has to step up" to the plate and resume financial responsibility for the four programs, Harlan said.

He said the city was "grossly mistreated" in the Home Rule plan. One of the "dumbest" moves was when D.C. agreed to take control of what has become a $2 billion pension liability. "It's going to eat your lunch," Harlan said the control board will tell Congress.
The report also will say that the District has been repeatedly cheated out of key sources of revenue because of its role as nation's capital, Harlan said.
For instance, most states have laws that permit them to recover abandoned property, including millions of dollars of unclaimed AMTRAK national train service passenger tickets, Harlan said.
AMTRAK, however, lobbied Capitol Hill and blocked D.C. from recovering from $10 million to $20 million in unclaimed tickets, Harlan said.

Harlan said the board's report also will say that the city needs more sources of revenue. The five-member board will study such options as imposing a controversial commuter tax on Virginia and Maryland residents who work in the District.
